blocks.x: Okay, Mr. Dominant, you might give your name on here again.
Alright, you want me to give my name, Bill? Daddy Dominant. Cornelius.
Can you tell me a little bit about your teacher, Manuel Perez?

I can tell you a lot about him, Bill. Manuel Perez was a very patient man giving lessons. And he's a very accomplished musician, a good musician. One man, if you didn't know all of your lessons, you missed one measure, he'd send you back home and give you the same lesson, or he wouldn't stand for your lesson. He'd tell you, he said, you're supposed to know your lesson when you get here. And I don't care whoever you put, whatever they put me, a piece of music. Mr. Perez, he'd read it first time. I see him play First Sight, Il Trivatar in the dance floor, at the Deluxe Cafe, First Sight. And I think he's one of the best colors ever.
Okay, you were talking about, you mentioned first of all that at the end of the other reel about old man Tio, Papa Tio, used a bad tone when he conducted.
He used a bad tone when he directed.
What kind of an orchestra did he conduct? Do you remember hearing any concerts?
Well yeah, he played all those heavy overtures, operas, you know opera numbers. He conducted them beautiful too. He really was marvelous to them. I think he was the greatest in the awards.
And the musicians who were in his big orchestra?
Yeah, they had Armand Piron, Peter Bocard, Nanya Perez, George Moray, Big Gasper, George Field, Shalini. He had Cartel on drums. And Cartel played timpanis too. Played what? Timpanis.
Oh, timpanis.

Oh yeah? Controlled the good musicians. That's why I can understand how his boy become a tenor saxophone. I thought he would think I'd say he's five years old. He plays clarinet some. Clarinet some. And he's a tenor sax. Very good tenor sax. And he had, let's see this, he had old man Gasper, old Gasper playing bass.
What about, can you tell a bit more about old Gasper?

Old Gasper, well I remember him when he was playing with Robey Shows Band Bass, orchestra, not the band. Played bass violin, strictly a bass violin man, and a good bass violin. And uh, did you know that going at Machine Bill? No, I remember. He played, I saw him play about four or five jobs. Once with many, twice with many careers. And he also played with George Moray, bass violin. He had a little concert. I think it was on Tulane Avenue.
Well I was going to ask these concerts at the Keough and all of them, Dave, where would they be? What kind of an auditorium?
Well they had it in the, in the, uh, Narkeeson Hall, Franz Ami Hall. North Carolina Hall. Yes, they had it. And you pay so much to go in.
People sit there and...

Enjoy that music, that classic, that high class stuff. But them same guys can come out and get in the orchestra and play jazz music too. But they play that melody. You see, they were used to playing melodies. They let the people understand what they were doing. You have to look, sometime I look, I saw, when I saw old man, uh, Gaspar, old Gaspar playing in an orchestra. And they give them choruses. And he talk about picking bass violin. He picked it beautiful. You wouldn't hear the string hit up against the finger roll. Beautiful. Jazz too. I think that's going in the machine.

Hold on, I don't hurt, the storm won't hurt that I don't think. Well, that kind of... Instead of picking up all the rain, you hear the rain on here and the, uh, thunder. I guess that won't be the tornado they predicted maybe anyway, we hope not.

So, them kind of fellas, I can tell you a lot about them, because I know them, I work with majority of them. Now we couldn't come to Jimmy Noon. I work with Jimmy Noon. My last recording on the deck was, you remember, with Jimmy Noon. Jimmy Noon and everybody. Johnny Dotson. My last recording on the deck. Johnny Dotson and Jimmy Noon. Jimmy Noon's a good musician. Read clarinet parts like nobody's business. I mean clarinet parts. And Johnny Dots could read clarinet parts. Very few clarinet parts you can find read clarinet parts. They'd read upper corner parts the matter. And of course they'd be able to improvise it, you know, jazz it the way they want. But when you put a clarinet part, like in parades and stuff, you got strictly clarinet. You have a lot of... Sometimes you come across 64 notes, 64 notes. You can hear those clarinet parts. Very fast. Similar to flute, yes. And Bab Frank. Great flutist. He was only flutist in New Orleans. And that's what old man Papa Dio had for flutists in that... in that symphony orchestra. Bab Frank. Great flutist. Never could play clarinet. And Jimmy Noon, I worked with Jimmy Noon plenty of times. Worked with him on gigs. I worked with him at the Paradise Cafe. I worked with him at the Apex Club. Paradise Cafe on Indiana 31st. The Apex Club on 31st and Calumet opposite the Sunset Cafe. I know what they all can do. And I played one job with Barney D. Gardner. When I worked with King Oliver.
Barney is your cousin. My cousin.

One job with Barney. He was busy, I was busy. The only one who had that after hour dance, you see. At the Sherman Hotel. I'll never forget that. That's why I worked with Barney. And Albert Dix was too. Wasn't that one learned under Lorenzo Dio. He's in New York. There's two in New York that learned under Dio. Orma Simeone and Albert Dix today. Good clarinet.
Can you tell us about Jimmy Brown? Jimmy Brown bass violin.
That was Manning's regular bass violin player. Jimmy Brown. Jimmy Brown.
Read music too. What style did he play? Did he use the bow or did he pick?
He used the bow but he didn't move picking. Beautiful picking. Tone. No slapping. Pick it.
Suda Renard.
He's Andrew Colvin Leonard. He can tell you about it. The more time musician. Oh he came from New Orleans.
He came from New Orleans too.
We ought to maybe interview him.
Let me make a note of him.
I don't know where Suda Renard lived. The last time I knew he lived was on Indiana.
Yeah we had trouble locating him two years ago. I know. Three years or more ago.
And Suda worked with us quite a while. That's another good one.
Can you tell us a little bit more about Tubby Hall? No.

Tubby Hall was a great rhythm drummer. Read music fair. Didn't really like Baby Dotts. I've got to give the old man credit. Baby Dotts can read music. Tubby Hall had a roll on a drum that's practically near as good as contral. And that's why Baby always wanted to make a roll like Tubby Hall. Tubby Hall made a roll like Downs. Norman Downs that's dead. That's another one. And I don't know where he got that roll from. Cause he learned in the contral. But I don't know where he stole it from contral or what. For contral toy. He had no smooth.
Tubby was younger than Minor.
Minor. Tubby's younger than Minor. He died.
You like Tubby's player better?

I like Tubby's player better than Minor. Cause Minor's good. But I like Tubby. That roll used to get me. And when he'd be rolling that rhythm with that foot. Look. It was pitiful. I'm telling you. You had to go. Keep his foot going.
Yeah.
No not fast. Not fast. You know what I'm going. Just a regular beat. You know like that. More than that. But it's like that. Like that.
No no. I meant four beats. Yeah.
Four beats.
Just like that.
Rhythm going. Yeah rhythm going. That's. Roll. He loved to roll that rhythm. And don't give him a Boston either. He was good on those Boston. Yeah. He could use them cymbals and everything.
Hit them cymbals.
That's a beautiful. That's. Don't. Cause there's nobody like Baby Dots. Baby Dots. Baby Dots. I still say. I take my boy. I'm not mad at him.
Baby Dots.

And Baby Dots. take my boy there. I'm not mad at him. Baby Dots. And Baby Dots, if drummers would read music like Baby Dots, and these folks I'm telling you about, young boys that's coming up, Bill is never going to knock anybody higher. But if they're going to try to knock that drum head, that bass drum front head to the back head, the way they're kicking them drums nowadays all that noise, they're not going any places. I'm telling you, they're not going any places, no further than the air. It's too bad to see them coming up like that. Because no such a thing as hitting a drum like that like that. That don't make sense. They don't give you a chance to carry stone. They're meeting each other too quick. The right way is this. Yeah, not too fast. No, not too fast, not too slow. If they're playing it fast, you can go fast. But they just want, and then when they're doing that, they're kicking it. They have got that heel here, and the foot up here. They're kicking it like that. They heel up. And that's what makes it sound bad. Because a bass drum, the Meister, man, she's got to get a rhythm with that bass violin. Yeah, which is right. Anybody know music. Because Bro kicked about because of the drum. Bro, Sonny Grimm. He's opposite. It's a pull between the rhythm section. See, I'm going this way and you're going the other way. Cause of contrast. Get together. See, your bass drum, practice with your bass violin. Your snap drum, is with your trumpets. Because we come in contact with each other in different measures. That's your snap drum. You didn't know that, did you? Yeah, you've explained it before. See, I know that. Now, what else you want to know, Bill?
Well, there's a couple other fellas here on the list. Joe Oliver, can you tell us what kind of a fella he was?

Fine fella. Swell guy. Full of fun. I work right opposite. Louie and I work opposite. And don't think, cause Louie and I was across the street. Joe Oliver had Bob Schauffer. And he also had Kid Ory. He had Joyce Field there, too. He had Kid Ory with him. Don't think the plantation was packed. Like our place was packed. Both in cabaret right opposite each other. It was packed. Danny had the apex across the street after hours. All the places would be packed. It was a good day. Yeah, it was a good day. Bob Schauffer was with him. Bob Schauffer was with Joe. He stayed with Joe a long time.
Same Bob Schauffer. Now, Joe was full of fun. Full of fun.

Was it easy to get along with? Easy to get along with. My estimation. He used to come across there, joke with us. Always had some joke. He asked me one day, what size hat you wear? I said, I wear a seven. He said, no, you wear a twelve and a half. I said, alright, kid. Then he'd do this at Louie. He said, Louie, apart from you, you can smell the rice cooking in China. And hold his hand up to his nose? To his nose, yeah. Full of fun. He was life of the pie. What was he said to Louie? Smell the rice cooking in China.
Louie knew what he meant then. Yeah, he knew what he meant. And he hold his finger up.
And he had to laugh. He was so comical. Louie had to laugh himself. Louie knew what he meant. He wasn't sure.
Louie knew what he meant. Did you know Joe's wife or...
Yeah, I did. I did. Very nice person. I don't know why she moved.
She's still in New Orleans. I never met her. I don't know if she's in New Orleans.
She's in Chicago. Even her daughter. I don't know where they went. They said her daughter was in New York the last time.
Yeah, I think so.
But I don't know where they went to, where Mrs. Oliver. Joe died in Topeka, Kansas, I think.
No, I think Savannah, Georgia.
Savannah, Georgia?
Yeah, down in Georgia.
Yeah, well, somewhere he died. Savannah, Georgia. But Joe's a good musician. He played a few parades with many parades. The same King Oliver.
Yeah.
Yeah, he's on a lot.
Do you remember if he was very good in those old days in New Orleans?
Very good.
Very good. You heard him first.
Heard him first. I played a picnic right alongside of Joe. He took all my people away from me. Yes, indeed. You know, I had them pavilions on the lake.
Oh, yeah.
They played picnics on the pavilions. People dancing like that. Well, Joe was right next to me. I said, you're about a block away from me?
Yeah.
He took all my folks away from me.
They all went over to hear him.
Yeah, we had to close up the place.
So we did that.
Played a lot of corners. Joe played a lot of corners. And he had longer wind than any man I've seen in the car.
More wind?
More wind.
Yeah.
Could blow a long.
Yeah.
Could blow a long time. Longer. Longer than Louis. Because when he came with that blues he had there, he had a, I think it's a 12 or 16-bar break.
Oh, yeah. Snagging.
That's the one that throwed us. Snagging.
Snagging.
It snagged Louis and I. With the look.
It throws us. Was his tone more powerful than Louis? No. Than Louis and other players? No.
He didn't have the tones more powerful than Louis. It made them more powerful than I, but he had a nice tone.
Did Joe use a mute very much? Yeah.
Very much.
What kind of a mute did he use?
A little silver mute. A little, uh. Long silver mute.
A long silver mute.
Yeah. He used that quite a bit. Because it was easier to blow than this short mute here. You see? The short mute here. It's kind of a strainer. He used a short mute like this. A con mute. Yeah.
A little con. Yeah. A little light bulb. You have one of those con mutes here too. Yeah.
You see? He used that to use his plunger. Then he used this. This is a light mute.

Oh, he put in this con mute. Yeah. The brass, started brass one. You see? I'll just show you. I'll never know. It's blown. It's blown. Yeah. I'm not blowing it. So you can blow it easy and I'll turn it down if you like.
No.
I just want to show you. Go ahead.
I just want to show you.
Yeah. That won't. That'll be good to have it on the table actually. I'll turn it down a little bit if you blow it. And then stick that little mute in and then use the plunger. Mm-hmm.
See? That's what he used. And Joe used to make high notes with those. It's just plunging. But it's hard.
This is harder than this one. Yeah, that con nude. That con nude is supposed to be a hard one to go.
It is. Because you can see the different tone with this nude and that nude. Excuse me? Excuse me? That's a long silver.

Long silver. Yeah. D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D&D D& D&D D&D D& D&D D& D&D D& D&D D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D& D&
Think about it. When we used to take a tin can and hang it on that.
Oh yeah.
On our horn with a piece of wire on it.
Just a wire and hang it on an ordinary tin can.
Yeah, a tin can. And hang it on there. That's what it sounds like.
Yeah.
Same thing. See? Yeah. It sounds just like that tin you put on your horn.
Did Joe ever use a derby hat?
Yeah. Use a derby hat. He hold it long ways. Like that. Yeah. We all use it. See? Hold your belt there.
Hold the belt and a couple of fingers around. Yeah. And blow it. Blow right in that derby.
If you want to make a better effect on a derby, you put your derby, half of your horn out.
Well, half the horn open and half...
Half in the derby.
Half in the derby.
Beautiful. Yeah. That's how we use it. Better for the use derby over there.
Did Manuel Perez ever use any of those nukes and things like that?
Yeah. Manuel used a nukes. And you know he used to use the nukes on waltzes.
Oh yeah. Beautiful waltzes.
Well, you left your plunger out.
Yeah. Did they use that plunger back in New Orleans too? Is that something that worked here later? No. It's something that worked here.
Worked up here. See that plunger? Same thing as taking a can. Yeah. Same thing. They do that with the tin can? Tin can. We used to do it with the tin can.
Did you ever see anybody do it with the coconut shell? No, never did.
Herb Moran.
Yeah? That Herb Moran.
I never see anyone do it with the coconut shell. No. They're not telling you that story.
Use it like a plunger. Hold out half of the coconut shell.
Yeah. Well, how it sounds like that?
Pretty good. Pretty good, eh? Yeah.
Never heard of that. He must be heard I couldn't buy a plunger. I don't know.
Well, let's see. If there's anything you can tell about Johnny Dodds that you've done. No.

No, no, no, no. You're talking about my boy, Johnny Dodds. Well, Johnny Dodds. I haven't heard of Clanness player yet, but the United States of America got a style like Johnny Dodds. Am I right, Bill? That's right. That's one. Johnny, what I liked about Johnny had its own style. He didn't try to imitate Benny Goodman. Didn't try to imitate Benny Biggert. Lorenzo Teo, Papatio, Backe, Sidney Dance, Fane, no nobody. He was Johnny Dodds in person. And only Johnny Dodds. Who'd never be forgotten because he had a style of his own. And he had a beautiful tune. And I used to go crazy when he played in that low register. A lot of Clanness players don't like to play in that low register because it's harder than the upper register. Guitars, it's difficult.
And Johnny mastered that role.

And I worked with him over 12 years together. You know that. He's a growing guy. Jokes, part, strictly business. And when they bring music up there on the bandstand and pubes, he would say, can you play it? That's your part. That's your part. That's your part. That's your part. Ready? Let's go. No rehearsals. The only way to rehearse went there was make records. Went to rehearse for records. Part when you were playing in his orchestra, fella come for that reason. Give you your parts. That's another one. To my estimation, if Johnny would hear all that record that's going on that progressive music, he'd go crazy. He'd go crazy. Johnny had a style of his own beat. Johnny had a good tune on the records too. Good tune. And could read music. Don't forget that.
Is there anything else you could tell about Johnny? What kind of a person he was? What his hobbies were? And what else he did?
Well, Johnny's hobby was eating a lot of sweets.
He ate a lot of sweets.
Yeah, that was his hobby.
What about any sports? Did he follow anything? Baseball.

White Sox fan. He died a White Sox fan. He didn't think there was another team in the whole world like the White Sox. He had go to baseball games. He went through a lot of games. He loved baseball. He taught baseball. He read baseball. He wasn't. That was me.

Anything else about him that is... Any of the jobs you played on? You've talked before on the tape from me about Johnny and the different jobs you've had. Is there anything else about him? When did you first meet him? Did you hear him in New Orleans? Did you hear him in New Orleans?
No, I never heard Johnny in New Orleans. I heard Johnny up here at the Royal Garden with King Oliver.
Was he as good the first time you heard him in Mr. Oliver as later when he worked with you?
Yes, yes.
But those old records you can't always tell about, but I wonder how he found it. Good, good. It was good then.

Very good. And baby was very fast. Very fast. That's what made that record. Baby Dots made that sound like two drums. Them drum solos, you know, you call it just drum. It sounded like two drums to me. But it was baby by himself. Baby was a streak of lightning.
Yeah, it's like lightning away against the ring. Yeah. There's a couple of other people here I was going to ask about. One briefly about Lizzie Miles.

I went to school with Lizzie Miles. Her name was Lizzie Landry. Her and I was in the same room. And I hope when you go to New Orleans, tell them you saw Dominic Dillacone play that went to Mary Lee's school with you.
The school was what, Mary?

Mary Lee's school. That's on Mary Lee between Oakwood and Vilry. Her name is Lizzie Landry. Her and I was together in this room. Riley's room, the teacher. And Mr. Raggio's room, that's the principal. You understand that? And we used to talk a lot. But I never knew Lizzie could sing. I never knew her sing. I took her to Chicago. I found out she could sing. But when she came to Chicago, she was married to that Pajot boy. That was her husband. He was running on the road. Then she left. And when Lizzie come back, they was living on the Vincennes. I saw her sitting around. Vincennes near Fort... Tate. Yeah? Yeah. She said, I kind of stepped like a doorway. And she said, hello, Natty. I said, hello Liz. I said, what are you doing here? You haven't got no time? She said, no, well. She said, I just wanted to get away for a while, you know. I said, how's the old man, Pajot? He said, oh, he's alright. He said, still on the road. That's the time my husband was on the road. But I knew the whole family. Pajot family. He was a very fine fellow. I don't know if they're together now, yes or no. She still uses that name. Pajot? I never met him. She still uses that name. He's famous. He's a nice guy. He's a nice guy. I don't know if they're together now, yes or no.
She still uses that name. Pajot? Pajot. I never met him. She still uses that name. He's famous.
He's a nice looking fellow.
I never met him.

He looked like a Mexican. Oh, he didn't be part English. Very nice fellow. And when I saw, I was surprised to see it, because when I saw her, when I left school, I lost track of Lizzie. Lizzie was thin. And when I saw that TV, you can tell her when I saw that TV, I didn't know that was on until I didn't recognize Lizzie. I said, well, Liz is my old school mate right there. Lizzie. Can you tell a little bit about Tony Jackson? No. Very good musician. I'll never forget it was on a Saturday night.
Tony Jackson sold Pretty Baby for $50 on a Saturday night.

I don't think he was working on a Saturday night. I don't think he was working on a Saturday night. I don't think he was working on a Saturday night. I don't think he was working at the dealer, at the, wait, wait. No, not with Matt Perez. Down below that. Eli? Eli. Eli number one. Near 35th street. 3400 block State Street on the west side, on the east side of the street of State Street. And he wasn't right that day. He sold it. He composed the words and the music. The words and the music. Sold $50. The man made about a million dollars off the record. Off that song. But I don't think he knew he wasn't right that night, Bill, when he sold it. The fella laid in the shed and weighed him. He knew, well, he kind of drank some, you know. He loved gin. That was his drink. He got that number for $50. He made a million dollars.
Was he known mostly as an entertainer and singer here on the piano play?
He was a singer, piano player, played with the orchestra too. Good piano player.
What was the style like on piano? Almost like Jellarole Martin.
I like Jellarole Martin. And I work with Jellarole Martin too. That's why I work with Jellarole Martin.
I know your first record just made it.
Jellarole Martin. London Blues, I think it was.
London Blues, the Sunday.
Sunday Sweetheart. That's the time Buster Bailey, Zoo Robinson. We had Johnny Sincere guitar. Who was playing bass? I think Bill Johnson was playing bass. I'm not mistaken. The Jellarole Martin.
Could it have been the Horace Eubanks song?

No, I could have had a record though with Horace Eubanks. That London Blues, the Sunday Sweetheart, that was with Buster Bailey. Buster Bailey. Buster Bailey, that's in New York now. That played with John Kirby's band.
Zoo on trombone.
Zoo on trombone. Man, that was a nervous guy too. He was so nervous.
Pull up and show his socks.
Yeah, show his socks, show everything.
Nervous, just nervous.

Good musician. Come on out, come on out. They played some good bass since then. They played good bass. And give them a solo to play a nice solo. Beautiful. But I don't know who taught Zoo Robinson. And I have it in me.
Somebody's name is Alil, maybe I'm not sure. But I don't know who taught him.
I'm not going to tell you no story. No. No, it's not me telling a story. I'm trying to tell you everything and the facts about it.
Yeah, but all we want to know is what you know is that. What about Buddy Johnson?

Buddy Johnson trombone player. I worked with him. The time Manion sent me on job with him. He was a very nice fellow inspiration. Quiet guy. Little bit of fellow he was. He played with Manion Barrett's brass man too, don't forget. Played all those marches. He ain't doing marches. Just imagine what Manion had. Big gas for Buddy Johnson trombone and Joe Field. Three devils up in front there. Now you know he had some good men, eh? Yeah. That's why they call it the Imperial Brass Band. But they're all good musicians. And the last thing I want to tell the boys, whoever going to listen to this record better, please learn music and learn everything pertaining to music. I want that man. And forget that trash pop.
There's a couple other men here. Richard M. Jones, Miney. Miney Jones.

I worked with him in Chicago. I worked with him in New Orleans. Well, you know yourself. My last recording was with Richard Miney Jones on the Decca Company. That was the last record I made with Jimmy Noon and Johnny Dodson. And both of them died.
I never heard him play much piano solos. Was he good on piano?

Very good on solos. Moneyy Jones could play some nice solos with him. Very good. He composed a lot of numbers. And he'd write it too. A lot of people didn't think Moneyy Jones knew music. But he'd write out that music. Moneyy Jones. I'm not going to down him. Another boy I worked with in New Orleans too, he's in that nice pal, but I don't know if he played with Walter Decker.
Oh no. He's still living. Still living.
No Walter's still living? Yeah. He looked simple.
What about P. Ron?

Well, Armand P. Ron, the best violinist right down in New Orleans, he was. And he could play jazz. Him of course. He'd play any kind of music. He was a complete musician. But one thing that you can't shake like my sister Kate, that's Louie Armstrong's number.
That's what I heard too. Louie told me that.
Louie's Armstrong's number, because P. Ron told it to me himself. And Clarence Williams told it to me himself.
You understand me?
Yeah. They got it away from Louie, I don't know for how much. Very cheap.
I think $25 or $50. Something like that.
I don't know. I can't tell you the price, but I'm going to tell you the price.
Maybe $50. Louie told me that.
And they made money off of that number.
Yeah.

But when you talk about I want to pick around for violin, opera, jazz, anything you want to play. Anything you put before those guys. They played Peter Bocard's nice violin play too. Peter Bocard's very good violinist.
Now did you hear Barney Bigard's father played violin didn't he? Do you remember him, Emil? No, that's his uncle.

His uncle I guess. Well Emil was in no class with those fellas. He wasn't? No. Emil Bigard was kind of heavy on these boys. He didn't have to touch those fellas. They could have bound both of them and everything. Yeah. Bound and bore in for the people. Because of people. They knew that. It looked like anywhere they finger fall that was right. A lot of bound them faster. Cause in all them opera numbers they had bound them both too. Come across that. Thank you.

segments.chapter: New Orleans teachers and classical musicians
segments.title: Opening and Manuel Perez as a patient, sight-reading teacher
segments.summary: Dominique gives his name, then describes teacher Manuel Perez: strict about lessons, an accomplished reader who sight-read at the Deluxe Cafe.

segments.chapter: New Orleans teachers and classical musicians
segments.title: Papa Tio's conducting and his opera orchestra
segments.summary: Tio directed heavy overtures and operas well; Russell asks about the musicians in his orchestra.

segments.chapter: New Orleans teachers and classical musicians
segments.title: Musicians in Tio's orchestra and bassist Old Gaspard
segments.summary: Dominique names Tio's orchestra members, mentions Tio's son on saxophone, and recalls Gaspard as a fine bass violinist.

segments.chapter: New Orleans teachers and classical musicians
segments.title: Concert halls and classical players who also played jazz
segments.summary: Concerts were held in halls with paid admission; the same classical players could play jazz melodically, Gaspard picking bass beautifully.

segments.title: Jimmy Noone, Johnny Dodds, Bab Frank and Chicago clubs
segments.summary: Dominique praises Noone and Dodds as clarinet readers, recalls flutist Bab Frank, his Chicago jobs with Noone, and a job with Barney Bigard.

segments.title: Bassist Jimmy Brown and Suda Renard
segments.summary: Jimmy Brown was Manning's bass violin player who bowed and plucked with no slapping; Suda Renard is a New Orleans musician worth interviewing.

segments.title: Tubby Hall, Baby Dodds and drumming technique
segments.summary: Dominique compares Tubby Hall and Baby Dodds, praises their rolls and reading, and criticizes modern drummers' loud bass drum kicking.

segments.title: Joe Oliver as a fun-loving man; his wife and death
segments.summary: Oliver was full of jokes, played opposite Dominique and Louis in Chicago cabarets; talk of his wife, daughter and where he died.

segments.title: Hearing Joe Oliver in New Orleans: picnics, wind and the break
segments.summary: Oliver drew away Dominique's picnic crowd at the lake pavilions, had long wind, and his blues break snagged Louis and Dominique.

segments.title: Joe Oliver's mutes, plunger and derby demonstration
segments.summary: Dominique and Russell handle mutes on the table: long silver, con mute, plunger, tin can and derby hat effects Oliver used.

segments.title: Manuel Perez's mute use, plunger origins and the coconut shell
segments.summary: Perez used mutes on waltzes; the plunger was a Chicago-era thing like the tin can, and Dominique never saw a coconut shell used.

segments.title: Johnny Dodds's individual style and bandstand manner
segments.summary: Dominique admires Dodds's unique low-register tone, says he worked with him over twelve years, and describes his no-rehearsal business manner.

segments.title: Johnny Dodds's hobbies and first hearing him with Oliver
segments.summary: Dodds loved sweets and the White Sox; Dominique first heard him at the Royal Garden with Oliver, and praises Baby Dodds's speed.

segments.title: Lizzie Miles as a school friend, and her husband Pajot
segments.summary: Dominique went to school with Lizzie Landry (Lizzie Miles), brought her to Chicago, and recalls her husband and meeting her again.

segments.title: Tony Jackson selling Pretty Baby for $50
segments.summary: Jackson, a singer and pianist, reportedly sold Pretty Baby for $50 while drinking at a Chicago State Street cafe.

segments.title: Jelly Roll Martin and the London Blues recording with Buster Bailey and Zutty Robinson
segments.summary: Dominique recorded London Blues and Sunday Sweetheart with Jelly Roll Martin, Buster Bailey, a nervous Zoo Robinson and others.

segments.title: Buddy Johnson and the Imperial Brass Band, with advice to learn music
segments.summary: Dominique worked with trombonist Buddy Johnson and recalls the Imperial Brass Band lineup, then urges young players to learn music.

segments.title: Richard M. Jones and his last Decca recording
segments.summary: Dominique worked with Jones in Chicago and New Orleans, made his last record with him, and defends his ability to write music.

segments.title: Armand Piron and the sale of Shimmy Like My Sister Kate
segments.summary: Piron was New Orleans' best violinist; Dominique and Russell agree the song was Armstrong's, bought cheaply by Piron and Clarence Williams.

segments.title: New Orleans violinists: Peter Bocage and the Bigards
segments.summary: Peter Bocage is praised as a violinist; Emile Bigard is discussed as Barney Bigard's uncle and a heavier player.
